papers.title: ToolCUA: Towards Optimal GUI-Tool Path Orchestration for Computer Use Agents
papers.research_area: Computer Use Agents, GUI Automation, Tool Use
papers.abstract: Current Computer Use Agents (CUAs) typically rely either on pure GUI interaction or on pre-defined tool APIs, limiting their adaptability. ToolCUA proposes a framework for optimal GUI-Tool path orchestration, enabling agents to dynamically choose between GUI operations and tool calls at each decision step. The paper introduces a path planning algorithm, curated training data, and benchmark evaluations that demonstrate how hybrid orchestration achieves higher task success rates with lower action cost than GUI-only or tool-only baselines on complex computer use tasks.
papers.summary: ToolCUA addresses the fundamental challenge of deciding when a Computer Use Agent should interact with a GUI versus call a specialized tool API. Rather than forcing agents into one mode, the framework builds an orchestration layer that plans the optimal hybrid action path for each task. It introduces curated training trajectories mixing GUI screenshots and tool calls, along with a benchmark that rewards path efficiency alongside task completion. Experiments show that hybrid GUI-Tool agents significantly outperform pure GUI agents on multi-step computer tasks, particularly where tool calls can shortcut tedious UI navigation.
key_contributions: GUI-Tool hybrid path orchestration framework for Computer Use Agents
Path planning algorithm that dynamically selects between GUI actions and tool API calls
Curated training data combining GUI interaction traces and tool call sequences
Benchmark evaluating both task success and action-path efficiency for CUAs

papers.title: MAI-UI Technical Report: Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents
papers.research_area: GUI Agents, Foundation Models, Web Automation
papers.abstract: The development of GUI agents could revolutionize the next generation of human-computer interaction. Motivated by this vision, we present MAI-UI, a family of foundation GUI agents spanning the full spectrum of sizes, including 2B, 8B, 32B, and 235B-A22B variants. We identify four key challenges to realistic deployment: the lack of native agent–user interaction, the limits of UI-only operation, the absence of a practical deployment architecture, and brittleness in dynamic environments. MAI-UI addresses these issues with a unified method- ology: a self-evolving data pipeline that expands the navigation data to include user interaction and MCP tool calls, a native device–cloud collaboration system routes execution by task state, and an online RL framework with advanced optimizations to scale parallel environments and context length. MAI-UI establishes new state-of-the-art across GUI grounding and mobile navigation. On grounding benchmarks, it reaches 73.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 91.3% on MMBench GUI L2, 70.9% on OSWorld-G, and 49.2% on UI-Vision, surpassing Gemini-3-Pro and Seed1.8 on ScreenSpot-Pro. On mobile GUI navigation, it sets a new SOTA of 76.7% on AndroidWorld, surpassing UI-Tars- 2, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Seed1.8. On MobileWorld, MAI-UI obtains 41.7% success rate, significantly outperforming end-to-end GUI models and competitive with Gemini-3-Pro based agentic frameworks. Our online RL experiments show significant gains from scaling parallel environments from 32 to 512 (+5.2 points) and increasing environment step budget from 15 to 50 (+4.3 points). Finally, the native device-cloud collaboration system improves on-device performance by 33%, reduces cloud model calls by over 40%, and preserves user privacy. papers.summary: MAI-UI presents a family of foundation GUI agents (2B, 8B, 32B, 235B-A22B) designed around four real-world deployment challenges: lack of native agent-user interaction, UI-only operation limits, missing practical deployment architecture, and brittleness in dynamic environments. The system combines a self-evolving data pipeline (expanding navigation data with user interaction and MCP tool calls), a device-cloud collaboration system that routes execution by task state, and an online RL framework with parallel environment scaling. MAI-UI achieves state-of-the-art results: 76.7% on AndroidWorld, 73.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, and 41.7% on MobileWorld, surpassing Gemini-2.5-Pro and UI-Tars-2, while the device-cloud system reduces cloud calls by 40% and improves on-device performance by 33%.
key_contributions: Family of foundation GUI agents at 2B, 8B, 32B, and 235B-A22B scales
Self-evolving data pipeline incorporating user interaction and MCP tool call data
Native device-cloud collaboration system reducing cloud calls by over 40%
Online RL framework scaling to 512 parallel environments, achieving SOTA on AndroidWorld (76.7%) and ScreenSpot-Pro (73.5%)

papers.title: MCP-Bench: Benchmarking Tool-Using LLM Agents with Complex Real-World Tasks via MCP Servers
papers.research_area: MCP, Benchmarking, Tool-Use Evaluation, LLM Agents
papers.abstract: MCP-Bench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents on complex real-world tasks delivered through MCP servers. It covers diverse domains requiring agents to chain multiple tools across long interaction horizons. The benchmark exposes failure modes in current agents through metrics that go beyond simple accuracy — measuring multi-step reasoning, error recovery, and cross-server orchestration — providing meaningful differentiation among state-of-the-art LLM agent systems.
papers.summary: MCP-Bench is a 52-page benchmarking framework that systematically evaluates LLM agents on complex, real-world tasks executed through Model Context Protocol servers. Going beyond single-step tool-call correctness, the benchmark designs multi-step task scenarios requiring cross-server orchestration, error recovery, and long-horizon reasoning. It evaluates leading frontier models and reveals significant capability gaps in how current LLMs handle realistic MCP workflows, providing the community with a rigorous standard for measuring progress in tool-augmented agent systems.
key_contributions: Comprehensive MCP benchmark spanning diverse real-world task domains
Multi-step evaluation metrics covering error recovery and cross-server orchestration
Systematic exposure of failure modes in state-of-the-art LLM agents
Standardized harness for reproducible and comparable MCP agent evaluation

papers.title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
papers.research_area: MCP, Benchmarking, Tool Use, LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is emerging as a standard interface through which large language model (LLM) agents discover and invoke external tools. However, existing MCP evaluations fall short along three key axes: realistic multi-step workflows with cross-server orchestration, breadth across authentic MCP servers rather than mocks, and structured, reproducible claim-level scoring disentangled from agent verbosity or style. We introduce MCP-Atlas, a benchmark for measuring tool-use competency against production MCP servers. MCP-Atlas contains 1,000 natural-language tasks written and verified by human experts spanning 36 real MCP servers and 220 tools. Prompts do not specify servers, tools, or parameters, requiring agents to identify relevant tools among semantically plausible distractors and to compose multi- step, cross-server workflows. Each task is scored with a claim-level rubric, where final answers are scored against atomic factual claims grounded in tool outputs. This answer-centric scoring permits valid alternative tool-call trajectories to receive credit. We pair this with an 11-category diagnostic taxonomy that disentangles tool-call failures from cognitive failures in task understanding, synthesis, parsing, and stopping. Evaluating 20 frontier models from six providers under matched task-level conditions, we find pass rates up to 82.2% at a 0.75 claim coverage threshold and a clear three-tier performance structure. Automated diagnostics show that 63.3% of diagnosed failures are cognitive rather than tool-call related. Notably, several high-performing models fail after successful tool execution due to premature stopping or incorrect synthesis. We release the task schema, containerized harness, claim evaluator, and a 500-task public split, while reserving a 500-task private split to preserve leaderboard integrity. The code is at https://github.com/scaleapi/mcp-atlas.
papers.summary: MCP-Atlas is a 1,000-task benchmark built on 36 real (non-mock) MCP servers and 220 tools, written and verified by human experts. Tasks are expressed in natural language without specifying which servers or tools to use, forcing agents to discover relevant tools among distractors and compose multi-step, cross-server workflows. Scoring uses claim-level rubrics grounded in actual tool outputs, and an 11-category diagnostic taxonomy separates tool-call failures from cognitive failures (understanding, synthesis, stopping). Evaluating 20 frontier models reveals pass rates up to 82.2% and shows that 63.3% of diagnosed failures are cognitive rather than tool-related — meaning models often succeed at calling tools but fail at synthesizing results or knowing when to stop.
key_contributions: 1,000-task benchmark across 36 authentic MCP servers and 220 real tools
Claim-level scoring rubric disentangled from agent verbosity and response style
11-category diagnostic taxonomy separating cognitive vs. tool-call failure modes
Evaluation of 20 frontier models revealing cognitive failures dominate (63.3%) over tool failures

papers.title: Alita: Generalist Agent Enabling Scalable Agentic Reasoning with Minimal Predefinition and Maximal Self-Evolution
papers.research_area: Agentic Reasoning, MCP, Generalist Agents, Dynamic Planning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to autonomously perform complex, open-ended tasks. However, many existing frameworks depend heavily on manually predefined tools and workflows, which hinder their adaptability, scalability, and generalization across domains. In this work, we introduce Alita—a generalist agent designed with the principle of "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication," enabling scalable agentic reasoning through minimal predefinition and maximal self-evolution. For minimal predefinition, Alita is equipped with only one component for direct problem-solving, making it much simpler and neater than previous approaches that relied heavily on hand-crafted, elaborate tools and workflows. This clean design enhances its potential to generalize to challenging questions, without being limited by tools. For Maximal self-evolution, we enable the creativity of Alita by providing a suite of general-purpose components to autonomously construct, refine, and reuse external capabilities by generating task-related model context protocols (MCPs) from open source, which contributes to scalable agentic reasoning. Notably, Alita achieves 75.15% pass@1 and 87.27% pass@3 accuracy, which is top-ranking among general- purpose agents, on the GAIA benchmark validation dataset, 74.00% and 52.00% pass@1, respectively, on Mathvista and PathVQA, outperforming many agent systems with far greater complexity. More details will be updated at https://github.com/CharlesQ9/Alita. ∗These authors contributed equally to this work.
papers.summary: Alita is a generalist agent built on the principle 'Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.' It uses only one core problem-solving component (minimal predefinition) while enabling maximal self-evolution by autonomously generating, refining, and reusing Model Context Protocols (MCPs) from open-source resources. Instead of relying on hand-crafted tool libraries, Alita dynamically constructs its own capabilities at inference time. It achieves 75.15% pass@1 and 87.27% pass@3 on the GAIA benchmark — top-ranking among general-purpose agents — and scores 74.00% on MathVista and 52.00% on PathVQA, outperforming far more complex agentic systems.
key_contributions: Minimalist agent design with a single problem-solving component requiring no predefined tool libraries
Self-evolution mechanism: agent autonomously generates and reuses MCP tools from open-source resources
Top-ranking GAIA benchmark performance: 75.15% pass@1 and 87.27% pass@3
Demonstrated generalization to vision-language tasks (MathVista, PathVQA) without task-specific scaffolding

papers.title: Model Context Protocol Threat Modeling and Analyzing Vulnerabilities to Prompt Injection with Tool Poisoning
papers.research_area: AI Security, MCP, Prompt Injection, Threat Modeling
papers.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has rapidly emerged as a universal standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools and data sources. While MCP simplifies integration, it introduces significant client-side security vulnerabilities. This work conducts threat modeling of MCP implementations using STRIDE and DREAD frameworks across five key components: MCP Host+Client, LLM, MCP Server, External Data Stores, and Authorization Server. The analysis identifies tool poisoning — where malicious instructions are embedded in tool metadata — as the most prevalent attack vector. A systematic comparison of seven major MCP clients reveals significant gaps in static validation. A multi-layered defense strategy is proposed covering static metadata analysis, model decision path tracking, behavioral anomaly detection, and user transparency mechanisms.
papers.summary: This paper applies classical security threat modeling frameworks (STRIDE and DREAD) to the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, systematically analyzing five attack surfaces: MCP hosts/clients, the LLM itself, MCP servers, external data stores, and authorization servers. The central finding is that tool poisoning — embedding malicious instructions inside tool descriptions and metadata — is the most exploitable and impactful client-side vulnerability. Seven real MCP clients are compared for their validation and defense capabilities, revealing widespread gaps. The paper proposes a multi-layer defense strategy combining static metadata checks, decision path monitoring, anomaly detection, and improved user transparency to secure MCP-based AI deployments.
key_contributions: First systematic STRIDE + DREAD threat model applied across all five MCP component layers
Identification of tool poisoning as the primary and most exploitable client-side attack vector
Comparative security analysis of seven major MCP clients exposing insufficient validation
Multi-layered defense strategy: static analysis, decision path tracking, anomaly detection, and user transparency

papers.title: EnvFactory: Scaling Tool-Use Agents via Executable Environments Synthesis and Robust RL
papers.research_area: Tool-Use Training, LLM Fine-tuning, Synthetic Data, Agent Training
papers.abstract: Equipping LLMs with tool-use capabilities via Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL) is bottle- necked by two challenges: the lack of scalable, robust execution environments and the scarcity of realistic training data that captures implicit human reasoning. Existing approaches depend on costly real-world APIs, hallucination-prone LLM simulators, or synthetic environments that are often single-turn or depend on pre-collected documents. Moreover, synthetic trajectories are frequently over-specified, resembling instruction sequences rather than natural human intents, reducing their effectiveness for RL training. We introduce EnvFactory, a fully automated framework that addresses both challenges. EnvFactory autonomously explores and verifies stateful, executable tool environments from authentic resources, and synthesizes natural multi-turn trajectories through topology-aware sampling and calibrated refinement, producing grounded queries with implicit intents. Using only 85 verified environments across 7 domains, EnvFactory generates 2,575 SFT and RL trajectories. Despite using significantly fewer environments than prior work, which are often 5 times more, EnvFactory achieves superior training efficiency and downstream performance, improving Qwen3-series models by up to +15% on BFCLv3, +8.6% on MCP-Atlas, and +6% on conversational benchmarks including 𝜏2-Bench and VitaBench. By fully automating both environment construction and trajectory synthesis, EnvFactory provides a scalable, extensible, and robust foundation for Agentic RL.
papers.summary: EnvFactory is a fully automated framework for training tool-use agents via Agentic RL, addressing two core bottlenecks: lack of scalable execution environments and scarcity of realistic training data. It autonomously explores and verifies stateful, executable tool environments from authentic sources, then synthesizes natural multi-turn trajectories using topology-aware sampling and calibrated refinement — producing grounded queries with implicit intents rather than over-specified instructions. Using just 85 verified environments across 7 domains, EnvFactory generates 2,575 training trajectories and improves Qwen3-series models by up to +15% on BFCLv3, +8.6% on MCP-Atlas, and +6% on conversational benchmarks (τ2-Bench, VitaBench), outperforming prior work that uses 5× more environments.
key_contributions: Automated framework for discovering and verifying stateful executable tool environments
Topology-aware trajectory synthesis producing natural, implicit-intent training data for RL
Generated 2,575 SFT and RL trajectories from only 85 environments across 7 domains
Qwen3-series improvements: +15% on BFCLv3, +8.6% on MCP-Atlas, +6% on conversational benchmarks

papers.title: AgentWall: A Runtime Safety Layer for Local AI Agents
papers.research_area: AI Safety, MCP, Runtime Security, Local AI Agents
papers.abstract: The safety of autonomous AI agents is increasingly recognized as a critical open problem. As agents transition from passive text generators to active actors capable of executing shell commands, modifying files, calling APIs, and browsing the web, the consequences of unsafe, mistaken, or adversarially manipulated behavior become immediate and tangible. Existing AI safety work has focused primarily on model alignment, capability evaluation, and input filtering – but these approaches do not address what happens at the moment an agent’s intent becomes a real action on a real machine. This gap is especially acute in local deployment environments, where developers run agents directly against their own filesystems, credentials, and development infrastructure with little runtime control. This paper introduces AgentWall, a runtime safety and observability layer for local AI agents. AgentWall addresses the agent safety problem at the execution boundary: it intercepts every proposed agent action before it reaches the host environment, evaluates it against an explicit declarative policy, requires human approval for sensitive operations, and records a complete tamper-evident execution trail for audit and replay. AgentWall is implemented as a policy- enforcing MCP proxy and native OpenClaw plugin, and works across Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, and OpenClaw with a single install command. The central argument of this paper is that safe AI agent deployment requires not only better models but also runtime infrastructure that enforces explicit boundaries between agent intent and machine execution. We present the design, architecture, threat model, and policy model of AgentWall, show its effectiveness across representative local-agent safety scenarios, and discuss its limitations and relationship to complementary safety approaches. AgentWall is open-source and available at https://github.com/agentwall/Agentwall.
papers.summary: AgentWall is an open-source runtime safety and observability layer for local AI agents that operates at the execution boundary — the critical moment when an agent's intent becomes a real action on a real machine. Implemented as a policy-enforcing MCP proxy and native OpenClaw plugin, AgentWall intercepts every proposed agent action before it reaches the host environment, evaluates it against an explicit declarative policy, requires human approval for sensitive operations (shell commands, file writes, API calls), and records a tamper-evident execution trail for audit. It works across Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, and OpenClaw with a single install command, requiring no model modifications. The paper argues that safe agent deployment requires not just better models but explicit runtime infrastructure enforcing boundaries between agent intent and machine execution.
key_contributions: Runtime MCP proxy intercepting agent actions before host execution with zero model changes
Declarative policy model covering shell commands, file I/O, API calls, and credential access
Tamper-evident execution trail enabling audit and replay of all agent actions
Single-install deployment across Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, and OpenClaw

papers.title: MCPEval: Automatic MCP-based Deep Evaluation for AI Agent Models
papers.research_area: MCP, Agent Evaluation, Automatic Assessment, LLM Benchmarking
papers.abstract: The rapid rise of Large Language Models (LLMs)-based intelligent agents underscores the need for robust, scalable evaluation frame- works. Existing methods rely on static bench- marks and labor-intensive data collection, limit- ing practical assessment. We introduce MCPE- val, an open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based framework that automates end- to-end task generation and deep evaluation of LLM agents across diverse domains. MCPE- val standardizes metrics, seamlessly integrates with native agent tools, and eliminates manual effort in building evaluation pipelines. Em- pirical results across five real-world domains show its effectiveness in revealing nuanced, domain-specific performance. We publicly re- lease MCPEval1 to promote reproducible and standardized LLM agent evaluation.
papers.summary: MCPEval is an open-source evaluation framework that automates end-to-end task generation and deep assessment of LLM agents using the Model Context Protocol as its evaluation substrate. Unlike static benchmarks that require labor-intensive data collection, MCPEval standardizes metrics, seamlessly integrates with native agent tools, and eliminates manual pipeline construction. Empirical results across five real-world domains demonstrate its effectiveness at revealing nuanced, domain-specific agent performance, enabling reproducible and standardized LLM agent evaluation at scale.
key_contributions: Open-source MCP-based framework automating end-to-end task generation and agent evaluation
Standardized metrics framework integrating natively with agent tool ecosystems
Elimination of manual evaluation pipeline construction through automated orchestration
Empirical validation across five real-world domains revealing domain-specific performance nuances

papers.title: Sema Code: Decoupling AI Coding Agents into Programmable, Embeddable Infrastructure
papers.research_area: MCP, AI Coding Agents, Developer Infrastructure, Software Engineering
papers.abstract: AI coding agents have become central to developer workflows, yet every existing solution locks its reasoning capabilities within a specific delivery form (CLI, IDE plugin, or web app), creating barriers when enterprises attempt to reuse capabilities across heterogeneous environments. Sema Code presents an open AI coding framework built on the principle of being embeddable, pluggable, and framework-first. It completely decouples the core agent engine from all client layers, publishing it as a standalone npm library. Key mechanisms include multi-tenant engine isolation, adaptive context compression, multi-agent collaborative scheduling, four-layer asynchronous permission control, and three-tier ecosystem integration spanning MCP, Skills, and Plugins. The same Sema Core engine simultaneously powers a VSCode extension and a multi-channel messaging gateway (Telegram, Feishu), demonstrating true architectural versatility.
papers.summary: Sema Code decouples AI coding agent reasoning from its delivery form, publishing the core engine as a standalone npm library that any runtime can drive programmatically. The architecture enforces a clean separation between the agent engine and all client layers (CLI, IDE plugin, messaging gateway), enabling a single reasoning kernel to simultaneously power a VSCode extension and a Telegram/Feishu messaging bot. Eight key mechanisms are designed: multi-tenant isolation, FIFO input queuing, adaptive context compression, multi-agent scheduling, Todo-based process management, four-layer async permission control, three-tier MCP/Skills/Plugins integration, and a background task framework. This architecture allows enterprises to embed and reuse agent capabilities across heterogeneous engineering environments without forking codebases.
key_contributions: Embeddable agent engine published as a standalone npm library decoupled from all client layers
Eight architectural mechanisms: multi-tenant isolation, adaptive compression, multi-agent scheduling, and four-layer permission control
Three-tier ecosystem integration spanning MCP servers, Skills, and Plugin systems
Single engine simultaneously powering VSCode extension and multi-channel messaging gateway (Telegram, Feishu)

papers.title: MCP Safety Audit: LLMs with the Model Context Protocol
papers.research_area: MCP Safety, AI Alignment, Security Auditing, LLM Deployment
papers.abstract: To reduce development overhead and enable seamless integration between potential components comprising any given generative AI application, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2025d) has recently been released and, subsequently, widely adapted. The MCP is an open proto- col which standardizes API calls to large language models (LLMs), data sources, and agentic tools. Thus, by connecting multiple MCP servers–each defined with a set of tools, resources, and prompts–users are able to define automated workflows fully driven by LLMs. However, we show that the current MCP design carries a wide range of security risks for end-users. In particular, we show that industry-leading LLMs may be coerced to use MCP tools and compromise an AI developer’s system through a wide range of attacks, e.g., malicious code execution, remote access control, and credential theft. In order to proactively mitigate the demonstrated (and related) attacks, we introduce a safety auditing tool, McpSafetyScanner, the first such agentic tool to assess the security of an arbitrary MCP server. McpSafetyScanner uses several agents to: a) automatically determine ad- versarial samples given an MCP server’s tools and resources, (b) search for related vulnerabilities and remediations given such samples, and (c) generate a security report detailing all findings. Our work thus sheds light on serious security issues with general purpose agentic workflows, while also providing a proactive tool to audit the safety of MCP servers and address detected vulnerabilities prior to deployment. The described MCP server auditing tool, MCPSafetyScanner, is freely avail- able at: https://github.com/johnhalloran321/mcpSafetyScanner.
papers.summary: This paper demonstrates that the current MCP design carries serious security risks, showing that industry-leading LLMs can be coerced into using MCP tools to compromise developer systems through malicious code execution, remote access control, and credential theft. In response, the authors introduce McpSafetyScanner — the first agentic security auditing tool for MCP servers — which uses multiple agents to automatically determine adversarial samples for a given server's tools, search for related vulnerabilities, and generate a comprehensive security report. The tool is freely available and provides a proactive mechanism to audit MCP server safety before deployment, addressing a critical gap in generative AI application security.
key_contributions: Demonstration of critical MCP security risks: malicious code execution, remote access control, and credential theft via coerced LLMs
McpSafetyScanner: first agentic tool for automated security auditing of arbitrary MCP servers
Multi-agent pipeline: adversarial sample generation, vulnerability search, and automated security report creation
Open-source release enabling proactive pre-deployment safety auditing of MCP servers

papers.title: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey
papers.research_area: RAG, Knowledge Graphs, Information Retrieval, LLM Augmentation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has achieved remarkable success in addressing LLM challenges without retraining. However, complex relational structures among entities in databases challenge standard RAG systems. GraphRAG leverages structural information across entities for more precise and comprehensive retrieval, capturing relational knowledge and enabling more accurate, context-aware responses. This paper provides the first comprehensive overview of GraphRAG methodologies, formalizing the workflow encompassing Graph-Based Indexing, Graph-Guided Retrieval, and Graph-Enhanced Generation. It examines downstream tasks, application domains, evaluation methodologies, and industrial use cases, and explores future research directions.
papers.summary: This survey is the first comprehensive overview of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG), which extends standard RAG by incorporating structured graph knowledge to overcome the limitations of flat document retrieval. The paper formalizes GraphRAG's three-stage workflow: Graph-Based Indexing (constructing knowledge graphs, document graphs, or entity graphs from corpora), Graph-Guided Retrieval (traversing graph structure for relational context), and Graph-Enhanced Generation (feeding graph context into LLMs). It surveys core technologies and training methods at each stage, reviews downstream tasks and industrial applications, and identifies open research challenges — making it the definitive reference for this rapidly growing paradigm.
key_contributions: First comprehensive survey and formal taxonomy of GraphRAG methodologies
Three-stage workflow formalization: Graph-Based Indexing, Graph-Guided Retrieval, Graph-Enhanced Generation
Review of core technologies, training methods, downstream tasks, and industrial deployments
Identification of open research challenges and future directions in graph-augmented LLM generation

papers.title: Hybrid LLM: Cost-Efficient and Quality-Aware Query Routing
papers.research_area: LLM Inference Optimization, Query Routing, Cost Efficiency, Model Selection
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in most NLP tasks but also require expensive cloud servers for deployment due to their size, while smaller models that can be deployed on lower cost (e.g., edge) devices, tend to lag behind in terms of response quality. Therefore in this work we propose a hybrid inference approach which combines their respective strengths to save cost and maintain quality. Our approach uses a router that assigns queries to the small or large model based on the predicted query difficulty and the desired quality level. The desired quality level can be tuned dynamically at test time to seamlessly trade quality for cost as per the scenario requirements. In experiments our approach allows us to make up to 40% fewer calls to the large model, with no drop in response quality.
papers.summary: Hybrid LLM proposes routing user queries between a small (cheap, fast) model and a large (expensive, capable) model based on predicted query difficulty and a desired quality threshold. The router is trained to estimate whether the small model's response meets quality requirements; if not, the query is escalated to the large model. Critically, the quality threshold is a runtime parameter — not baked into training — allowing operators to seamlessly trade quality for cost at inference time without retraining. Experiments show up to 40% fewer calls to the large model with no drop in response quality across diverse NLP tasks.
key_contributions: Query routing framework dynamically selecting between small (edge) and large (cloud) LLMs
Difficulty-prediction router trained on quality signals to minimize large-model invocations
Runtime-tunable quality threshold enabling seamless cost-quality tradeoff without retraining
Up to 40% reduction in large-model API calls with no measurable quality degradation

papers.title: ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model
papers.research_area: LLM Alignment, Preference Optimization, RLHF, Training Efficiency
papers.abstract: While recent preference alignment algorithms for language models have demonstrated promis- ing results, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) re- mains imperative for achieving successful con- vergence. In this paper, we study the cru- cial role of SFT within the context of pref- erence alignment, emphasizing that a minor penalty for the disfavored generation style is sufficient for preference-aligned SFT. Build- ing on this foundation, we introduce a straight- forward and innovative reference model-free monolithic odds ratio preference optimization algorithm, ORPO, eliminating the necessity for an additional preference alignment phase. We demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that the odds ratio is a sensible choice for con- trasting favored and disfavored styles during SFT across the diverse sizes from 125M to 7B. Specifically, fine-tuning Phi-2 (2.7B), Llama-2 (7B), and Mistral (7B) with ORPO on the Ul- traFeedback alone surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art language models with more than 7B and 13B parameters: achieving up to 12.20% on AlpacaEval2.0 (Figure 1), 66.19% on IFEval (instruction-level loose, Table 6), and 7.32 in MT-Bench (Figure 12). We release code1 and model checkpoints for Mistral-ORPO- α (7B)2 and Mistral-ORPO-β (7B).3
papers.summary: ORPO introduces a reference-model-free approach to preference alignment that merges supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization into a single training phase. The core insight is that a minor odds-ratio-based penalty applied during SFT is sufficient to discourage disfavored response styles, eliminating the need for a separately trained reference model (as required by DPO, PPO, etc.). Validated across model sizes from 125M to 7B, ORPO fine-tuning on just the UltraFeedback dataset surpasses state-of-the-art models with 7B–13B parameters: achieving 12.20% on AlpacaEval 2.0, 66.19% on IFEval, and 7.32 on MT-Bench.
key_contributions: Reference-model-free preference alignment eliminating the need for a separate KL-regularization model
Unified single-phase training combining SFT and preference optimization via odds ratio penalty
Validated across 125M to 7B models on UltraFeedback, surpassing 13B-parameter baselines
SOTA results: 12.20% AlpacaEval 2.0, 66.19% IFEval, 7.32 MT-Bench with Mistral-7B

papers.title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
papers.research_area: LLM Routing, Inference Optimization, Cost Efficiency, Model Selection
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at a wide range of tasks, but choosing the right model often involves balancing performance and cost. Powerful models offer better results but are expensive, while smaller models are more cost-effective but less capable. To address this trade-off, we introduce a training framework for learning efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger and weaker LLM during inference. Our framework leverages human preference data and employs data augmentation techniques to enhance performance. Evaluations on public benchmarks show that our approach can reduce costs by over 2 times without sacrificing response quality. Moreover, our routers exhibit strong general- ization capabilities, maintaining performance even when routing between LLMs not included in training. This highlights the potential of our framework to deliver cost-effective, high-performance LLM solutions.
papers.summary: RouteLLM (ICLR 2025) trains lightweight router models to dynamically select between a stronger (expensive) and weaker (cheaper) LLM at inference time, leveraging human preference data and data augmentation. Four router architectures are explored: similarity-weighted ranking, matrix factorization, BERT classifier, and a causal LLM-based classifier. The framework achieves over 2× cost reduction without sacrificing response quality on public benchmarks. Notably, trained routers generalize across LLM pairs not seen during training, demonstrating the framework's robustness for real-world cost-efficient LLM deployment.
key_contributions: Training framework for learned routers using human preference data with data augmentation
Four router architectures: similarity-weighted ranking, matrix factorization, BERT classifier, causal LLM classifier
Over 2× inference cost reduction with no quality degradation across public benchmarks
Strong router generalization to unseen LLM pairs, enabling flexible deployment configurations

papers.title: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling
papers.research_area: Function Calling, Parallel Execution, LLM Agents, Tool Use Optimization
papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of the recent LLMs enable them to execute external function calls to overcome their inherent limitations, such as knowledge cutoffs, poor arithmetic skills, or lack of access to private data. This development has allowed LLMs to select and coordinate multiple functions based on the context to tackle more complex problems. However, current methods for function calling often require sequential reasoning and acting for each function which can result in high latency, cost, and sometimes inaccurate behavior. To address this, we introduce LLMCompiler, which executes functions in par- allel to efficiently orchestrate multiple function calls. Drawing inspiration from the principles of classical compilers, LLMCompiler enables par- allel function calling with three components: (i) a Function Calling Planner, formulating execution plans for function calling; (ii) a Task Fetching Unit, dispatching function calling tasks; and (iii) an Executor, executing these tasks in parallel. LLMCompiler automatically generates an opti- mized orchestration for the function calls and can be used with both open-source and closed-source models. We have benchmarked LLMCompiler on a range of tasks with different patterns of function calling. We observe consistent latency speedup of up to 3.7×, cost savings of up to 6.7×, and accuracy improvement of up to ∼9% compared to ReAct. Our code is available at https://github.com/SqueezeAILab/LLMCompiler.
papers.summary: LLMCompiler draws inspiration from classical compiler design to enable parallel function calling in LLMs. It decomposes a function-calling task into three components: a Function Calling Planner (formulates an execution DAG), a Task Fetching Unit (dispatches ready tasks), and an Executor (runs tasks in parallel). By identifying independent function calls and executing them concurrently, LLMCompiler achieves up to 3.7× latency speedup, 6.7× cost savings, and ~9% accuracy improvement over sequential ReAct-style execution. It works with both open-source and closed-source LLMs and automatically generates optimized orchestration plans.
key_contributions: Three-component parallel execution system: Function Calling Planner, Task Fetching Unit, and Executor
DAG-based dependency analysis enabling safe concurrent execution of independent tool calls
Up to 3.7× latency speedup and 6.7× cost savings over sequential ReAct baseline
Compatible with both open-source and closed-source LLMs with automatic orchestration optimization

papers.title: Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
papers.research_area: Multi-Agent Systems, Ensemble Methods, LLM Collaboration, Response Quality
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) demonstrate substantial capa- bilities in natural language understanding and generation tasks. With the growing number of LLMs, how to harness the collective expertise of multiple LLMs is an exciting open direction. Toward this goal, we propose a new approach that lever- ages the collective strengths of multiple LLMs through a Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) methodology. In our approach, we construct a layered MoA architecture wherein each layer comprises multiple LLM agents. Each agent takes all the outputs from agents in the previous layer as auxiliary information in generating its response. MoA models achieves state-of-art performance on AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench and FLASK, surpassing GPT-4 Omni. For example, our MoA using only open-source LLMs is the leader of AlpacaEval 2.0 by a substantial gap, achieving a score of 65.1% compared to 57.5% by GPT-4 Omni.1
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) constructs a layered multi-agent architecture where each layer consists of multiple LLM agents, and each agent uses all outputs from the previous layer as auxiliary context when generating its own response. This ensemble approach harnesses the collective expertise of diverse LLMs — acting as proposers in early layers and synthesizers in later layers. MoA achieves state-of-the-art performance on AlpacaEval 2.0 (65.1% vs. GPT-4 Omni's 57.5%), MT-Bench, and FLASK, demonstrating that open-source LLM collaboration can surpass proprietary frontier models.
key_contributions: Layered Mixture-of-Agents architecture where each agent aggregates all previous-layer outputs
Proposer-synthesizer role separation enabling progressive response refinement across layers
SOTA AlpacaEval 2.0 score of 65.1% surpassing GPT-4 Omni (57.5%) using only open-source LLMs
Flexible, heterogeneous-LLM-compatible framework with no model retraining required

papers.title: Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
papers.research_area: Reasoning, Chain-of-Thought, Prompting Strategies, LLM Problem Solving
papers.abstract: We introduce SELF-DISCOVER, a general frame- work for LLMs to self-discover the task-intrinsic reasoning structures to tackle complex reasoning problems that are challenging for typical prompt- ing methods. Core to the framework is a self- discovery process where LLMs select multiple atomic reasoning modules such as critical think- ing and step-by-step thinking, and compose them into an explicit reasoning structure for LLMs to follow during decoding. SELF-DISCOVER sub- stantially improves GPT-4 and PaLM 2’s per- formance on challenging reasoning benchmarks such as BigBench-Hard, grounded agent reason- ing, and MATH, by as much as 32% compared to Chain of Thought (CoT). Furthermore, SELF- DISCOVER outperforms inference-intensive meth- ods such as CoT-Self-Consistency by more than 20%, while requiring 10-40x fewer inference com- pute. Finally, we show that the self-discovered reasoning structures are universally applicable across model families: from PaLM 2-L to GPT-4, and from GPT-4 to Llama2, and share commonal- ities with human reasoning patterns.
papers.summary: SELF-DISCOVER is a general framework enabling LLMs to self-compose task-specific reasoning structures before tackling complex problems. The two-phase process first has the LLM select and adapt relevant atomic reasoning modules (e.g., critical thinking, divide-and-conquer, step-by-step analysis) into an explicit reasoning structure, then uses that structure to guide decoding. Compared to standard Chain-of-Thought (CoT), SELF-DISCOVER improves GPT-4 and PaLM 2 performance by up to 32% on BigBench-Hard and outperforms CoT-Self-Consistency by 20%+ while using 10–40× less inference compute. The self-discovered structures transfer across model families (PaLM 2-L → GPT-4 → Llama 2) and share commonalities with human reasoning patterns.
key_contributions: Two-phase framework: atomic reasoning module selection then explicit structure composition before solving
Up to 32% improvement over Chain-of-Thought on BigBench-Hard for GPT-4 and PaLM 2
Outperforms CoT-Self-Consistency by 20%+ using 10–40× less inference compute
Self-discovered reasoning structures transfer across model families and reflect human reasoning patterns

papers.title: M3-Bench: Multi-Modal, Multi-Hop, Multi-Threaded Tool-Using MLLM Agent Benchmark
papers.research_area: MCP Benchmarking, Multimodal Tool Use, Multi-Hop Reasoning, MLLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: We present M3-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating multimodal tool use under the Model Context Protocol. The benchmark targets realistic, multi-hop and multi-threaded workflows that require visual grounding and textual reasoning, cross-tool dependencies, and persistence of intermediate resources across steps. We introduce a similarity-driven alignment that serializes each tool call, embeds signatures with a sentence encoder, and performs similarity-bucketed Hungarian matching to obtain auditable one-to-one correspondences. On top of this alignment, we report interpretable metrics that decouple semantic fidelity from workflow consistency. The benchmark spans 27 servers with 232 tools, and provides standardized trajectories curated through an Executor & Judge pipeline with human verification; an auxiliary four large language models (LLMs) judge ensemble reports end-task Task Completion and information grounding. Evaluations of representative state-of-the-art Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) reveal persistent gaps in multimodal MCP tool use, particularly in argument fidelity and structure consistency, underscoring the need for methods that jointly reason over images, text, and tool graphs.
papers.summary: M3-Bench is the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate multimodal tool use under the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Unlike prior text-only MCP benchmarks that focus on linear API planning, M3-Bench addresses three critical real-world challenges: (1) visual grounding — agents must interpret images before parameterizing tool calls; (2) multi-hop reasoning — causally dependent tool operations spanning multiple steps; and (3) multi-threading — concurrent tool calls within a single step. The benchmark covers 27 MCP servers with 232 tools across 21 diverse tasks (e.g., Travel Comparison, Heatmap, Museum, Research Station). Evaluation uses a novel similarity-driven Hungarian matching algorithm to align predicted vs. ground-truth tool call trajectories, reporting metrics including Recall, Precision, Argument Similarity, Step Coherence, Order Consistency, Merge Purity, Task Completion, and Information Grounding. A 4-LLM judge ensemble is used for end-task quality assessment. SOTA MLLM leaderboard results show GPT-5 leads at 0.482 average score, followed by Grok 4 (0709) at 0.423 and GPT-5 Mini at 0.411, while weaker models like GLM 4.5v score only 0.141, revealing that all current models struggle significantly with multimodal MCP tool-calling — especially argument fidelity and structural consistency. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/EtaYang10th/Open-M3-Bench.
key_contributions: First benchmark for multimodal MCP tool use combining visual grounding, multi-hop, and multi-threaded tool workflows
27 MCP servers, 232 tools, 21 diverse real-world task scenarios
Similarity-driven Hungarian matching algorithm for auditable trajectory alignment
Interpretable multi-dimensional metrics: Argument Similarity, Step Coherence, Order Consistency, Merge Purity, Task Completion, Information Grounding
4-LLM judge ensemble for end-task evaluation with human verification
Comprehensive SOTA MLLM leaderboard revealing persistent gaps in multimodal MCP tool use
